summary: Canada is the world's second-largest country by area, located in northern North America, and is known for English–French bilingualism, its multicultural policy and magnificent natural landscapes.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population has grown rapidly in Canada, from under 5% in the 1971 census to about 35% in 2021. Postwar educational expansion and urbanization, the Quebec 'Quiet Revolution' of the 1960s in which the provincial government took over education and health care from the Catholic Church, and recent distrust of the churches stirred by the residential school scandals have all led many people to leave religion.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism arrived with French colonization of New France (present-day Quebec) in the 17th century, and after Quebec City was founded in 1608, orders such as the Jesuits and the Ursulines opened schools and hospitals. After Britain acquired New France in 1763, the Quebec Act of 1774 guaranteed freedom of Catholic worship, and the Catholic Church long dominated Quebec society. Irish immigrants in the 19th century and Italian, Portuguese and Filipino immigrants in the 20th century also increased the number of Catholics.

ranking.name: Other Christian denominations
ranking.description: Among other Christian denominations the largest is the United Church of Canada, formed in 1925 by the merger of the Methodists, Presbyterians and Congregationalists, followed by the Anglicans, Baptists, Orthodox and Pentecostals. In the British colonial period the Anglican Church was the officially supported church, and the Loyalists who moved north after the American Revolution also brought many Protestants, giving Protestantism the advantage in Ontario and the Atlantic provinces.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam already had a small number of records in the 1871 census, but its large-scale growth came after 1967, when Canada's immigration policy changed to a points system and racial restrictions were abolished. Immigrants and refugees from Pakistan, Lebanon, Iran, Algeria, Somalia and elsewhere have concentrated Muslims in big cities such as Toronto and Montreal.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: Hindus are mainly immigrants from India, Sri Lanka, Guyana and Trinidad after the immigration reform of 1967, and since 2000 skilled migrants and international students have continued to increase. They are concentrated in the Greater Toronto Area; for example, Brampton and Mississauga have many large Hindu temples.

ranking.name: Sikhism
ranking.description: Sikhs first passed through Canada with the British Indian army in 1897 at Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee, and in the early 20th century began to settle in British Columbia to work in forestry. In the 1914 Komagata Maru incident, hundreds of Indian immigrants were refused permission to land, reflecting the racial discrimination of the time. After 1967 Sikh immigration increased greatly, and today Sikhs are concentrated in Surrey in British Columbia and Brampton in Ontario.

religion.background: Canada's indigenous peoples (First Nations, Inuit and Métis) originally had diverse spiritual traditions. French colonization in the 17th century brought Catholicism and British colonization in the 18th century brought Protestantism, forming the two great Christian traditions of English and French Canada. From the 19th to the late 20th century, the government and churches jointly ran residential schools for indigenous children, forcibly assimilating them; the government formally apologized in 2008, and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission issued its report in 2015. Since the 1960s secularization and diverse immigration have changed the religious map, and the non-religious population has become the largest category.

language.official: English and French are the federal official languages.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English took root in Canada with British colonization in the 18th century and the northward move of the American Loyalists after 1783, and in the 19th century large numbers of English, Scottish and Irish immigrants made English the main language of most provinces. Canadian English blends features of British and American English; for example, it keeps the spelling 'colour', but its pronunciation is closer to American English. About 56% of the population have English as their mother tongue, and second-generation immigrants mostly switch to English.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French arrived with the founding of Quebec in 1608 and the colonization of New France, and after Britain acquired New France in 1763, the Quebec Act of 1774 guaranteed the rights of French-speaking residents. The Quiet Revolution of the 1960s in Quebec promoted French-language nationalism, the Official Languages Act of 1969 established English–French bilingualism as the federal official-language policy, and Quebec's Bill 101 of 1977 made French the only official language of that province. Today French speakers are concentrated in Quebec, New Brunswick and eastern Ontario.

ranking.name: Punjabi
ranking.description: Punjabi speakers are mainly Sikhs and some Hindu and Muslim immigrants; Punjabis were already working in British Columbia in the early 20th century, but large-scale immigration began in 1967. Today Punjabi is one of the most common immigrant languages in Canada, especially in Surrey in British Columbia and Brampton in Ontario, and there are also quite a few Punjabi-Canadian members of the federal Parliament.

ranking.name: Chinese (Mandarin)
ranking.description: Early Chinese speakers mainly spoke Cantonese; during the 1858 gold rush in British Columbia and the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway in the 1880s, large numbers of Cantonese immigrants came to Canada. From 1885 to 1923 the government levied a head tax on Chinese, and in 1923 it even passed the Chinese Immigration Act (Chinese Exclusion Act), which was not repealed until 1947. After 1967 immigrants from Hong Kong and Taiwan increased, and from the 1990s immigrants from mainland China increased greatly, so that Mandarin speakers now outnumber Cantonese speakers.

language.history: Canada has more than 60 indigenous languages belonging to over ten language families, such as Cree, Inuktitut and Ojibwe, but most are endangered under the forced assimilation policy of the residential schools. The French founded Quebec in 1608, and after Britain acquired New France in 1763, English and French coexisted and competed in Canada for a long time. The Official Languages Act of 1969 established the federal bilingualism policy, and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms of 1982 guaranteed the educational rights of English and French minority-language groups. Since 1971 Canada has pursued a multicultural policy, and today about a quarter of the population have a mother tongue that is neither English nor French.

ranking.name: Poutine
ranking.description: French fries are topped with rich gravy and then sprinkled with fresh cheese curds, which half-melt in the hot gravy and squeak when bitten.
ranking.history: Poutine originated in the 1950s in small diners in rural Quebec, and several towns contest the specific place of invention, such as Warwick and Drummondville. Quebec produces plenty of dairy, and cheese curds are a common local snack. It was first regarded as cheap country food and was even used to mock Quebecers, but from the 2000s, as restaurants promoted it, it became a national dish of Canada and also a symbol of Quebec cultural identity.

ranking.name: Maple syrup
ranking.description: An amber syrup made by boiling down and concentrating the sap tapped from sugar maple trees, with a distinctive caramel and woody aroma, poured over pancakes or used in cooking.
ranking.history: The indigenous peoples of eastern Canada were cutting the bark of maple trees in spring to collect sap and boiling it into sugar long before the arrival of Europeans. In the 17th century the French colonists learned the technique from the indigenous peoples, and maple sugar became an important source of sweetness for the inhabitants of New France. Today Canada produces about 70% of the world's maple syrup, the great majority of it from Quebec, and the maple leaf is also the symbol on the Canadian flag (adopted in 1965).

ranking.name: Butter tart
ranking.description: A small pastry tart filled with a semi-liquid filling of butter, sugar, syrup and eggs, sometimes with raisins or walnuts, sweet and rich.
ranking.history: The butter tart is a representative dessert of English Canada, and the earliest known recipe appeared in the Royal Victoria Hospital Cook Book published in Barrie, Ontario, in 1900. It is generally thought to have possibly been influenced by the pastry tradition brought by the 17th-century 'Filles du Roi' (young women sent to New France), but this claim is not conclusive. Today it is a classic dessert in bakeries and homes in Ontario and across Canada.

ranking.name: Nanaimo bar
ranking.description: A no-bake dessert of three layers: a base of crumbs made of chocolate, coconut and walnuts, a middle layer of custard buttercream, and a top layer of chocolate.
ranking.history: The Nanaimo bar is named after Nanaimo, a city on Vancouver Island in British Columbia, and the earliest known recipes appeared in local community cookbooks in the 1950s. Because it needs no oven, it became a convenient dessert for housewives and church events. In 1986 the city of Nanaimo held a contest to find the 'ultimate Nanaimo bar' recipe, and today it has become one of Canada's most representative desserts.

ranking.name: Tourtière
ranking.description: A meat pie baked in pastry, filled with ground pork, ground beef or game mixed with onion, potato and spices such as cloves and cinnamon.
ranking.history: Tourtière is a traditional Quebec dish, and its name may come from the French word 'tourtière' for the earthenware dish used for baking meat pies, or from the passenger pigeon (tourte) that was once used as the filling. In the 17th century French colonists brought the meat-pie tradition to New France and made it with local game. Today it is an essential dish at Quebec's Christmas Eve (réveillon) and New Year, and every family has its own inherited recipe.
